summary: The Last Safe Home is a platform that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite data and historical satellite images to monitor river erosion in Bangladesh, focusing on Monpura and Koyra. It helps people check how safe their homes and farmland are by showing risk scores, distance from the river, erosion rates, and estimated time before the river may reach them. Users can explore 2026 radar images with a time slider, compare land changes from 1988 to today, draw any area on the map to generate a detailed report, and download reports for local authorities. Our goal is to help families and authorities understand erosion risks early and make better decisions about protecting homes or relocating safely.
details:
What does the project do?

The Last Safe Home is a bilingual (English and Bangla) web platform that helps communities in coastal Bangladesh understand the risks of riverbank erosion. Focusing on Monpura Island (Bhola) and Koyra (Khulna), it uses NASA–ISRO NISAR radar data and historical satellite images to show how rivers are changing and how those changes may affect nearby homes and farmland.

Users can select a location to see its distance from the riverbank, erosion rate, flood frequency, and a Home Risk Score (0–100), along with an estimated range of years before the river may reach that location. They can also explore radar images over time, compare shorelines from 1988 to 2026, draw areas to analyze land loss and exposed buildings, and generate reports for local authorities.

How does it work?

We process NISAR L-band radar data to identify water and land, while Landsat images help track historical riverbank changes from 1988 to 2026. We measure shoreline retreat using transects, estimate flood frequency from available radar observations, and use NISAR interferometric data to estimate ground movement where data quality permits.

These factors are combined into a Home Risk Score:

Risk Score = 100 × (0.6 × Erosion Hazard + 0.3 × Flood Frequency + 0.1 × Ground Movement)

The platform also estimates how many years may remain before the river reaches a selected location, based on its distance from the riverbank and the estimated retreat rate. We compare water detection results with Sentinel-2 imagery and provide validation information on the platform.

Benefits and intended impact

Unlike optical satellites, radar can observe the Earth's surface through clouds and at night, making NISAR especially useful during the monsoon season. Our platform turns complex satellite observations into understandable information that families and local authorities can use.

Our goal is to help vulnerable communities prepare earlier, protect their assets, plan safer relocation, and make better-informed decisions before losing their homes and farmland. In the future, we aim to expand coverage and introduce Bangla SMS and voice alerts.

Tools and technologies

  • Satellite data: NASA–ISRO NISAR, Landsat, Sentinel-2.
  • Other datasets: OpenStreetMap, WorldPop, geoBoundaries.
  • Data processing: Python, NumPy, Xarray, Rasterio, RioXarray, GeoPandas, Scikit-image.
  • Backend: FastAPI.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Terra Draw.
  • Deployment: Docker, Render, Vercel, GitHub Pages.
  • Testing: Pytest, Vitest, Playwright.

What makes the project creative?

Our project uses one of the first NISAR datasets to address a practical human question: "How long might it be before the river reaches my home?" By combining new radar observations with 38 years of historical satellite data, we transform scientific measurements into simple, location-based risk information. We also communicate uncertainty through estimated ranges rather than presenting predictions as exact facts.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Accessibility: Bilingual support and a mobile-friendly interface.
  • Reliability: Satellite estimates are validated against other satellite imagery and clearly distinguished from ground-based engineering surveys.
  • Transparency: Risk scores, methods, and validation information are available to users.
  • Affordability: We use free, open satellite datasets and open-source technologies.

Use of AI: We used Claude and Claude Code for project planning, brainstorming, coding assistance, debugging, and creating video animations. Our team reviewed and tested the generated code.
